text:
**LiFePO4 is the better choice for most buyers.** Most current models use it, and it lasts much longer. NMC's main advantage is energy per pound, and that advantage shrinks in finished products.

**Why LiFePO4 usually wins**

- **Lifespan:** LFP models are commonly rated around 3,000 to 4,000 cycles to 80% capacity. Older NMC models are typically rated 500 to 800 cycles ([UnpluggedWatts](https://www.unpluggedwatts.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-power-station/), [OutageMath](https://www.outagemath.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc/)). Daily use would wear out an NMC unit in a few years, while an LFP unit would take most of a decade.
- **Failure behavior:** In a lab study of large cells pushed into overcharge, the LFP cells released smoke without flames, while all the NMC cells ignited ([UnpluggedWatts](https://www.unpluggedwatts.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-power-station/)). LFP is not fireproof, but it's the safer chemistry to keep indoors or in a vehicle.
- **Price:** The premium for LFP has mostly disappeared. The median price per Wh is about $0.55 for LiFePO4 versus $0.95 for NMC, and NMC now survives mainly in compact units and older designs ([PowerStationsReviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc)).

**Where NMC has an edge**

- **Weight:** NMC cells store more energy per kilogram. In finished stations, though, the gap is smaller, roughly 10 to 16% per pound in the data these sites compiled, because the inverter, case, and ports weigh the same regardless of chemistry ([OutageMath](https://www.outagemath.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc/), [PowerStationsReviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc)). Some sites claim NMC is about 20% lighter per kWh, but the finished-product numbers vary by model, so compare specs directly.

**Cold weather**

Chemistry matters less than you might expect. Many LFP and NMC stations both refuse to charge below 32°F (0°C), and the manual sets the real limits ([UnpluggedWatts](https://www.unpluggedwatts.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-power-station/)). Some sources say NMC is more prone to lithium plating when charged in the cold ([VoltVanguard](https://volt-vanguard.com/article/lifepo4-vs-nmc-battery-chemistry/)), but the manual is the authority.

**When NMC still makes sense**

- You need the lightest possible unit and will use it only a few times a year.
- You already own an NMC station that works. There's no need to replace it.

**Before you buy**

- Check the cycle rating's end point. "4,000 cycles to 80%" and "4,000 cycles to 70%" are not the same promise ([Enough Watts](https://enoughwatts.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc)).
- Choose capacity and output for your loads first, then chemistry. A long-lasting battery doesn't help if the inverter can't start your fridge ([PowerStationsReviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc)).

**Source note:** The sources disagree on some figures, such as NMC cycle counts (500 to 2,000) and thermal runaway temperatures. The more detailed guides cite lab studies, while others give rounder numbers without sources. I'd weight the first three guides above more heavily.
